Name: PrintDry Pro 2.0
Description: The PrintDry Pro 2.0 earns its place on max temperature alone — at 80°C it’s the only dedicated dryer in this comparison that meets the recommended drying temperature for PA/nylon (75–80°C), PC (80°C+), and exotic filaments like PVDF. The two-spool capacity is a workflow advantage for multi-material builds. The absence of a humidity sensor is the main gap — you’re running on time rather than feedback. Community context: underrepresented in mainstream dryer discussions but consistently recommended by PA and engineering filament builders who know their temperature requirements.
Verdict Label: Highest max temp in this comparison — the right pick for PA/PC/PVDF builders

Performance is equivalent to the Sunlu S2 at 70°C with active fan and humidity indicator. Community view: worth the premium if you’re deep in the Polymaker ecosystem and want the manufacturer’s explicit endorsement, or if build quality over the S2’s budget construction matters. Name: eSUN eBOX Pro
Description: The eSUN eBOX Pro is distinguished by its built-in filament weight scale, letting you track remaining spool weight without pulling it out mid-print. Feed port, humidity sensor, and temp display are all present. The critical limitation is the 55°C ceiling — well below what PA/nylon (75–80°C) and PC (80°C+) require. Community consensus: the scale is genuinely useful, but the temp ceiling makes this a PLA/PETG-only dryer. If you don’t regularly need the scale, the Sunlu S2 outperforms it for less money.
Verdict Label: Built-in filament scale is genuinely useful — but the 55°C ceiling limits what it can dry

Name: EIBOS Cyclopes
Description: The EIBOS Cyclopes is the performance pick in this category. Its convection heating design produces more even temperature distribution than the budget alternatives, and the 75°C ceiling enters the effective drying range for PA/nylon where the S2 falls short. Community verdict is clear: Sunlu S2 for value-conscious builders who primarily dry PLA and PETG; EIBOS for anyone printing hygroscopic engineering filaments regularly and wanting confidence in the result. At roughly 2× the S2 price, the upgrade justifies itself once PA, moisture-sensitive TPU, or ASA that’s been sitting open are part of your regular rotation.
Verdict Label: Performance benchmark — the upgrade from S2 when drying quality matters

Name: DIY Food Dehydrator (Cosori / Excalibur)
Description: Before purpose-built filament dryers existed, the 3D printing community adopted food dehydrators — and the approach still holds up. Cosori (round stackable trays, $50–70, ~72°C max) and Excalibur (rectangular, $150+, excellent even airflow, ~74°C+) are the most cited models. Remove the center post, place the spool in the tray, run at 65–70°C for 4–6 hours. Feed port requires drilling a small hole in the housing and installing a bowden coupler — community tutorials widely available. Excalibur in particular has more even temperature distribution than most dedicated filament dryers. Best choice if you already own one, or want the highest temp ceiling at the lowest cost per spool.
Verdict Label: The original community method — high temp, cheap, effective, needs a DIY feed port

Name: eSUN eBOX Lite
Description: The eSUN eBOX Lite is the budget floor — functional for keeping recently-opened PLA and PETG from absorbing ambient moisture, but with a 45°C ceiling it cannot rescue filament that has already absorbed significant moisture. Think of it as a heated dry box rather than a dryer. Community context: adequate for maintaining filament condition between print sessions; not the right tool if you’re starting with wet filament or printing hygroscopic engineering materials.
Verdict Label: Budget dry-storage box with slight warmth — maintenance drying only

Name: Sunlu FilaDryer S4
Description: The Sunlu S4 scales the S2’s proven active drying system to four simultaneous spools. Aimed at multi-material builders running an AMS, toolchanger, or high-volume print farms — the four independent feed ports let you print from any slot while the others dry. At $75 the per-spool cost is roughly equivalent to four individual S2 units, but the integrated form factor and single power connection is meaningfully cleaner. Same 70°C ceiling as the S2 applies throughout.
Verdict Label: Four-spool simultaneous drying — right pick for multi-material and high-volume builders

Name: Bambu AMS Dry Box
Description: The Bambu AMS is not a filament dryer — it’s a multi-spool buffer and sealed storage system integrated with Bambu’s multi-material printing workflow. It keeps loaded filament drier than open-air exposure but has no heating element and cannot rescue moisture-laden filament. Documented here as a reference and comparison point for crossover builders evaluating ecosystems: if your filament is already wet, you need a dedicated dryer before it goes into the AMS. Not a self-build ecosystem product.
Verdict Label: Bambu-only dry storage system — not a dryer, a sealed multi-spool buffer

Name: Sunlu FilaDryer S2
Description: The Sunlu FilaDryer S2 is the community’s default recommendation when budget is the constraint. For under $30 it delivers a PTFE feed port, active fan circulation, humidity sensor, and temperature display — all the features that matter. It performs well for PLA, PETG, and TPU within its 70°C ceiling. Community consensus: buy it if you’re starting out or need to dry occasional spools; upgrade to EIBOS when engineering filaments (PA, PC) are in regular rotation and drying quality is non-negotiable.
Verdict Label: Best value filament dryer — the community default under $30
